title: Kafka: scalability and sizing
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: What one broker can handle, why not to store blobs, how to scale with brokers and partitions, and the partition formula.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: Roughly what can one well-equipped Kafka broker handle?

options.text: About 1 TB of data and about 1 million messages per second.
options.why: Right: hand-wavy but useful.

options.text: About 1 GB and 100 messages per second.
options.why: Far too low; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: About 1 PB and a billion messages per second.
options.why: Far too high for one broker.

options.text: It depends only on the topic name.
options.why: It depends on size and hardware.

questions.explanation: Estimate your numbers first; if the design fits one broker, scaling is not the conversation.

questions.prompt: What message size is recommended for Kafka?

options.text: Under 1 MB; the hard limit is message.max.bytes.
options.why: Right: small messages are processed quickly.

options.text: Several gigabytes per message.
options.why: Kafka is not a file store.

options.text: Exactly one byte under normal operating conditions.
options.why: No such rule; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Any size, with no impact on memory.
options.why: Large messages add memory pressure.

questions.explanation: Keeping messages small uses the network better.

questions.prompt: A video must be transcoded by workers. How should it travel through Kafka?

options.text: Upload it to S3 and send a small Kafka message with its link.
options.why: Right: keep the file out of Kafka.

options.text: Put the whole video in one Kafka message without any extra configuration.
options.why: That breaks the small-message design.

options.text: Split it into thousands of messages without a key in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Order and reassembly would suffer.

options.text: Email it to each worker.
options.why: Not a design; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: This is the claim-check pattern: send the address, not the blob.

questions.prompt: What are the two ways to scale Kafka?

options.text: Add more brokers and choose a good partitioning strategy through the key.
options.why: Right: the key is the main interview focus.

options.text: Increase message size and reduce partitions under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That works against scaling.

options.text: Add more consumers than partitions in a group in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Extra consumers sit idle.

options.text: Turn off replication to save capacity.
options.why: That harms durability.

questions.explanation: Managed Kafka often scales brokers for you, so the key remains the decision.

questions.prompt: You add brokers but the topic has too few partitions. What happens?

options.text: The extra brokers sit idle because partitions cannot use them.
options.why: Right: partitions are the unit of spread.

options.text: Messages are automatically re-split across new brokers as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Partitions must exist first.

options.text: The new brokers store copies of old messages only in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Replication is separate.

options.text: The topic is deleted.
options.why: Not a real effect; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Topics need enough partitions to use the new brokers.

questions.prompt: Using partition = hash(key) % num_partitions, a key hashes to 17 and there are 3 partitions. Which partition?

options.text: Partition 2, since 17 mod 3 is 2.
options.why: Right; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Partition 0 without any extra configuration.
options.why: 17 mod 3 is not 0; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Partition 1 in a typical production setup.
options.why: 17 mod 3 is 2, not 1; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Partition 5.
options.why: Only 0 to 2 exist; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: The default hash function is murmur2.

questions.prompt: True or false: if your estimated load fits inside one broker, scaling Kafka is not a relevant conversation.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: do the maths before you scale.

options.text: False
options.why: It is not relevant if the numbers fit one broker.

questions.explanation: Estimate throughput and storage first; roughly 1 TB and 1 million messages per second per broker is the yardstick.

questions.prompt: Why do you usually think about scaling one topic at a time?

options.text: Different topics have different needs, so busy topics get more partitions and quiet ones stay small.
options.why: Right: a per-topic decision.

options.text: Topics all share exactly the same traffic for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: They differ; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: A cluster can only have one topic.
options.why: It can have many; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Partitions cannot be added to a topic as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: They can; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: Confluent Cloud and AWS MSK handle much of the scaling for you.
